quote: From what I'm seeing, it looks like there's a pretty tall tree in the front yard putting some shade. Is that right?
stewart_read: Rep proactively pulled Google Maps to check shading before asking — this is above-baseline diligence in the verify section, not just box-checking.
coaching_implication: Reinforce this as a repeatable habit — call it out positively so the rep knows this level of prep is valued and expected.

quote: Now our program, what it does is it actually saves you money immediately, and the only requirement is that you have a credit score above 650.
stewart_read: The schema's documented threshold is 670; this rep stated 650, an unresolved 20-point drift. This is not a customer-facing failure in this call (customer confirmed she qualifies either way) but it is a live policy-consistency problem the schema explicitly flags for this exact call.
coaching_implication: Confirm with Kenny whether 670 or 650 is the current active threshold and correct whichever rep/script version is wrong — this call is the documented drift exemplar.

quote: When I talked to somebody before, they had told me that it could probably go on my garage roof, but the garage roof would need to be redone because... it's 20 years old.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers that she's had a prior solar conversation with someone else, including specific technical detail (garage roof placement, age). Rep never asks who that was, what company, or what else was discussed — pure competitive intel left on the table.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have judged the detail sufficiently captured for design purposes and prioritized moving the call forward — but this doesn't require probing depth, it requires one follow-up question.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask 'who told you that?' or 'was that another solar company?' in the moment — costs 10 seconds, gives the closer real competitive context.

quote: my bill would have been 500 this summer had I not
stewart_read: Customer hands the rep a strong number ($500 peak summer bill) unprompted. Rep acknowledges ("Was that was that 500 bill, that's probably the highest, I'm assuming") but never returns to it as leverage when booking the appointment.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest missed flip on the call — coach the rep to close with something tying the appointment to that $500 peak, e.g., referencing it as the number the design will attack.

quote: customer: Oh, I do. For you? Yeah. Perfect.
stewart_read: Credit qualifier resolved instantly and cleanly — not a miss itself, but it's immediately followed by rep moving to bill collection without building any curiosity about what the design could show her. Neutral procedural moment, flagged for context only.
coaching_implication: No action needed here specifically — noted as a transition point where a curiosity-building line could have been inserted.

quote: Don't wanna save my bill. I just wanna log in.
stewart_read: Real customer frustration surfaces here mid-login-struggle in a public store. Rep did not acknowledge the frustration verbally or accelerate the instructions until later — a mild empathy gap during a live friction point, not a catastrophic one since the call recovered.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have been intentionally staying quiet to avoid adding pressure while she worked through the login — a legitimate patience strategy.
coaching_implication: When a customer voices frustration mid-task, a brief acknowledgment ("no rush, take your time" or clearer next-click guidance) reduces the chance of the customer disengaging entirely.

quote: Please have whoever text me and then say, you know, call me at this number.
stewart_read: Customer stipulates a real logistical constraint (dead zone, needs a text-first contact method) for the follow-up call to succeed. Rep acknowledges but the button-up never restates the appointment with the standard elements (hour block, no-driving/computer instruction, explicit 'is that fair?').
coaching_implication: Flag for closer: this appointment has a real show-risk factor (phone dead zone) that must be worked around with a text-first contact protocol, not just noted and forgotten.

quote: Well, awesome, Kelly. I'll get things scheduled. If you need me, you've got my number. Just let me know. But we'll plan on talking tomorrow at eleven.
stewart_read: Call ends with a day/time locked (tomorrow at 11) but skips the full button-up: no hour-block statement, no no-driving/computer instruction, no explicit 'is that fair?' handshake — just a passive close.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the customer already raised her own logistical constraint (dead zone) and the rep addressed that specifically, the rep may have judged the standard button-up redundant — but the schema treats these elements as required regardless.
coaching_implication: Drill the full button-up sequence as a checklist regardless of how smoothly the call is going — the hour-block and computer-readiness lines are tied to no-show reduction and were skipped here.
